statement: The prime $13$ has the property that reversing its digits gives a different prime, $31$. How many two-digit primes have this property?

choices.misconception: I counted each pair once, 13 and 31, 17 and 71, 37 and 73, 79 and 97, but both primes in each pair have the property.
I also counted 11, but reversing 11 gives 11 again, which is not a different prime.
I also counted 11 and 19, but 11 reverses to itself and 91 = 7 times 13 is not prime.
I counted all 21 two-digit primes without checking their reversals.

hints: The reversed number must also be a prime, so it cannot end in an even digit or in $5$.
That means both digits of the original prime are $1$, $3$, $7$ or $9$. List the two-digit primes that use only those digits.
The list is $11, 13, 17, 19, 31, 37, 71, 73, 79, 97$. Now reverse each one and check.

solutions.reliable: A two-digit prime ends in $1$, $3$, $7$ or $9$, and its reversal, also a prime, must end in one of those digits too, so both digits come from $\{1, 3, 7, 9\}$. The primes built from those digits are $11, 13, 17, 19, 31, 37, 71, 73, 79, 97$ (the others, $33, 39, 77, 91, 93, 99$, are not prime). Now reverse: $11$ gives itself, which is not a different prime, and $19$ gives $91 = 7 \cdot 13$. The other eight work in pairs: $13$ and $31$, $17$ and $71$, $37$ and $73$, $79$ and $97$. The answer is $8$.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
